H&P NOTE
Author: undefined
==================================================

S — Subjective

ID: 54M
CC: Abdominal pain, N/V x2 days

HPI: 54-year-old man with HTN and extensive prior abdominal surgery (trauma ex-lap with splenectomy, appendectomy, cholecystectomy, ventral hernia repair) presents with 2 days of progressively worsening abdominal pain with abdominal distension, nausea, and multiple episodes of emesis with inability to tolerate PO. Symptoms worsening over time. No peritoneal-type pain reported. Given operative history, presentation is most consistent with adhesive SBO until proven otherwise; need to rule out closed-loop/strangulation.

ROS: +abdominal pain/distension, +N/V, +poor PO. Denies fever/chills per report. No GI bleeding reported.

PMH: HTN
PSH: Ex-lap/splenectomy (trauma), appy, chole, ventral hernia repair
Meds: Not available (currently NPO)
Allergies: Not listed
FHx/SHx: Not provided

O — Objective

VS: T 98°F, BP 106/78, HR 104, RR 16, SpO₂ 97% RA
Gen: Mild distress, uncomfortable, nauseated
Abd: Distended, tympanitic, mild diffuse TTP, no rebound/guarding
(Other systems: noncontributory/not documented)

Labs: WBC 12, lactate 1.4, K 3.1, Cr 2.4 (baseline ~1.0)
Imaging: Pending
Current management: NPO, NGT to LIS, maintenance IVF

A — Assessment

54M with multiple prior laparotomies presenting with clinical SBO (distension + vomiting + tympany) without peritonitis. Mild leukocytosis/tachycardia likely from dehydration/pain. Normal lactate and benign abdominal exam argue against ischemia/strangulation currently, but he remains high risk given surgical history. Complicated by pre-renal AKI and hypokalemia from GI losses.

P — Plan (surgical style)
1) Suspected adhesive SBO (rule out closed-loop/strangulation; consider recurrent ventral hernia)

Continue NPO, NGT to LIS; document NG output and character.

Resuscitation: IVF, replace NG losses 1:1 as needed.

Imaging: CT A/P—given Cr 2.4, start non-contrast; if clinical concern for ischemia/transition point/closed loop increases, discuss risk/benefit of IV contrast with medicine/nephrology.

Serial exams: q4h abdominal checks; monitor for escalating pain, peritonitis, persistent tachycardia, rising WBC/lactate.

Analgesia/antiemetics: judicious opioids; ondansetron PRN.

If partial SBO and stable: consider water-soluble contrast challenge (Gastrografin) per institutional protocol after CT/if no aspiration risk.

Escalation criteria: worsening exam, increasing lactate, hemodynamic instability, CT concern for closed-loop/ischemia → OR.

2) AKI (likely pre-renal from vomiting/third spacing)

Fluids: isotonic bolus then maintenance; target UOP >0.5 mL/kg/hr.

Avoid nephrotoxins; hold ACEi/ARB/diuretics if applicable.

Trend BMP (q6–12h initially), consider UA/urine lytes if not improving.

3) Hypokalemia (K 3.1) from emesis/NG losses

Replete K (IV while NPO); check/replete Mg.

Repeat BMP after repletion; telemetry if aggressive replacement or additional derangements.

4) HTN

Hold home PO agents while NPO and borderline BP; treat only if severe HTN with short-acting IV PRN.

clinicalNotes.title: Admission H&P
clinicalNotes.content:
S — Subjective
Demographics

Daniel Edwards, 67-year-old man.

Chief Complaint

Hyperglycemia and hyponatremia with concern for volume overload/heart failure.

History of Present Illness

Adult male with known type 2 diabetes on home basal/bolus insulin (home regimen glargine 45 units qHS + lispro 10 units with meals) admitted from the ED for severe hyperglycemia and hyponatremia. Initial blood glucose 415 mg/dL (confirmed on accucheck) with normal anion gap and normal lactate (0.8), arguing against DKA. Serum sodium 123 mEq/L (likely partially glucose-related; corrected Na ~128). BNP returned markedly elevated at 1400, prompting discontinuation of IVF and initiation of 2 L/day fluid restriction. Given concern for hypoglycemia on a controlled inpatient diet and reported outpatient dietary nonadherence, he was restarted on lower-dose insulin: glargine 15 units qHS and lispro 5 units with meals. BMP/BNP, EKG, and CXR ordered and pending (BNP resulted as above).

Review of Systems (positives/negatives only)

ROS limited by available documentation; patient denies fever/chills, chest pain, abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, dysuria, and focal neurologic deficits. Additional symptom details (e.g., dyspnea, orthopnea, edema) not yet documented—will obtain on admission.

Past Medical History

Type 2 diabetes mellitus (insulin-requiring)

Possible heart failure/volume overload physiology suggested by BNP 1400 and fluid restriction (prior HF history not provided)

Possible hypertension (BP elevated on arrival; chronic history not provided)

Past Surgical History

Not documented.

Medications

Home: glargine 45 units qHS; lispro 10 units with meals (per notes)

Inpatient (current): glargine 15 units qHS; lispro 5 units with meals; fluid restriction 2 L/day

Allergies

Not documented.

Family History

Not documented.

Social History

Tobacco/alcohol/drugs, living situation, baseline functional status not documented.

O — Objective
Vital Signs

BP 165/89, HR 85, RR 11, SpO₂ 95% RA, Temp 98.6°F

General Appearance

Not fully documented at time of note.

Physical Exam (by system)

Comprehensive exam not yet documented; will complete on admission.

CV/Pulm: pending (need JVP, rales, edema assessment)

Abd/GI: pending

Neuro: pending

MSK/Ext: pending for edema/perfusion

Skin: pending

Labs

CBC: WNL

BMP: sodium 123, potassium 4.2, chloride 89, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L; anion gap 10 mmol/L; glucose 415 mg/dL; BUN 14 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL.

Lactate: 0.8

BNP: 1400

Corrected sodium for hyperglycemia: ~128 mEq/L (estimate)

Imaging/Studies

EKG: ordered, pending

CXR: ordered, pending

A — Assessment & P — Plan
1) Severe hyperglycemia in T2DM (no clear DKA by current data)

Rationale/Ddx: BG 415 with normal AG and lactate → DKA less likely; need to assess for ketosis, hyperosmolar state, infection/ischemia triggers, medication nonadherence. Risk modifier: outpatient dietary nonadherence; inpatient controlled diet may lower insulin needs.
Diagnostics

STAT: VBG, beta-hydroxybutyrate/serum ketones, UA for ketones/glucose

Serum osmolality (evaluate for HHS)

A1c, Mg/Phos

Screen precipitant as indicated: troponin (esp. with BNP elevation), infectious eval if symptoms
Therapeutics

Continue current basal/bolus glargine 15 qHS + lispro 5 with meals with correctional insulin; titrate daily to goal 140–180 inpatient

If HHS/DKA features emerge → transition to insulin infusion protocol
Monitoring

POC glucose AC/HS (q4–6h if NPO)

Monitor K/Mg/Phos closely with insulin adjustments
Disposition

Diabetes education + ensure discharge regimen and supplies; assess barriers/adherence

2) Hyponatremia (Na 123; likely partially translocational from hyperglycemia; consider hypervolemic hyponatremia)

Rationale/Ddx: Corrected Na ~128 suggests glucose effect; BNP 1400 and fluid restriction suggest possible hypervolemic hyponatremia (HF). Must exclude true hypotonic hyponatremia etiologies.
Diagnostics

Repeat BMP q6–12h initially

Serum osmolality, urine osmolality, urine sodium

Consider TSH and AM cortisol if unclear etiology
Therapeutics

Maintain 2 L/day fluid restriction

Treat underlying driver (optimize HF management; improve hyperglycemia)

Avoid rapid correction: target ≤6–8 mEq/L per 24h
Monitoring

Strict I/O; daily weights

Neuro checks if Na falls or symptoms occur

3) Suspected acute decompensated heart failure / volume overload physiology (BNP 1400)

Rationale/Ddx: Markedly elevated BNP plus IVF discontinued + fluid restriction suggests concern for ADHF; need objective confirmation (CXR, exam, possible echo). Consider renal dysfunction/age/AF as BNP confounders (not provided).
Diagnostics

CXR, EKG (pending)

Troponin x1–3 (rule out ischemic trigger as indicated)

CMP, Mg

Review prior TTE if available; order TTE if no recent study or change in status
Therapeutics

IVF discontinued (already done)

Continue fluid restriction 2 L/day

If clinical congestion on exam/CXR: start IV loop diuretic (e.g., furosemide) with electrolyte monitoring; if not congested, hold diuresis pending objective assessment
Monitoring

Telemetry

Strict I/O, daily weights, daily BMP while diuresing
Disposition

Optimize GDMT if HF diagnosis confirmed and hemodynamics/renal function allow; arrange close follow-up

4) Hypertension (165/89)

Rationale/Ddx: Elevated BP on presentation; unclear chronicity. In HF physiology, BP control reduces afterload and congestion risk.
Diagnostics

Verify home antihypertensives (med rec)
Therapeutics

Treat contributing pain/anxiety; if persistently elevated, initiate/adjust antihypertensive guided by renal function and HF status (after med rec)
Monitoring

Trend BPs; avoid overly rapid lowering without end-organ damage signs

clinicalNotes.title: H&P Note
clinicalNotes.content:
H&P NOTE
Author: undefined
==================================================

Chief Complaint

“Vomiting and now my heart feels weird and I’m dizzy.”

History of Present Illness

Samantha Brooks is a 14-year-old female with a history of anxiety, celiac disease, and migraines admitted for intractable vomiting and dehydration, now with new palpitations and dizziness in the setting of QT-prolonging medications and likely electrolyte losses.

Three days prior to admission, she developed multiple episodes of non-bloody, non-bilious emesis and was unable to tolerate oral intake. She denies fever, diarrhea, abdominal trauma, sick contacts, or recent travel. She has been compliant with her gluten-free diet and denies any known gluten exposure. No urinary symptoms. She tried small sips of water and electrolyte drinks at home but vomited most attempts.

She presented to the ED appearing dehydrated but hemodynamically stable. Initial BMP was within normal limits, and she received IV fluids and antiemetics. Given persistent vomiting and poor PO tolerance, she was admitted for IV fluids and gut rest.

Home medications (continued on admission):

Hydroxyzine for anxiety

Amitriptyline for migraines

Both are known QT-prolonging agents.

Inpatient PRN medications ordered and used:

Ondansetron IV/PO PRN for nausea

Prochlorperazine IV PRN for nausea

Lorazepam IV PRN for nausea/anxiety

Over the first hospital day she continued to have frequent vomiting (≈5–6 episodes) and minimal PO intake. She received several doses of ondansetron and prochlorperazine, in addition to her scheduled amitriptyline and hydroxyzine.

Earlier in the day, vitals were normal and exam was notable only for dry mucous membranes. BMP at that time was normal.

Current episode:

This afternoon, nursing was called when Samantha reported feeling “dizzy” and that her heart feels weird/skips beats. She also felt lightheaded when sitting up. She denied severe chest pain, shortness of breath, or syncope, but clearly appeared more pale and anxious and continued to feel nauseous.

Current vitals at that time:

BP 96/58

HR 112 (irregular)

RR 20

SpO₂ 96% RA

Temp 98.6°F

On exam she was pale, anxious, holding an emesis bag, and her heart rhythm felt irregular on auscultation.

Given concern for arrhythmia in the setting of vomiting + multiple QT-prolonging drugs, a repeat BMP, magnesium level, and EKG were obtained:

BMP: K 2.7 (low), otherwise stable

Mg: 1.3 (low)

EKG: QTc 540 ms with ventricular ectopy (PVCs)

She has had no prior history of syncope, known arrhythmia, or congenital heart disease. No known personal or family history of sudden cardiac death.

At the time of this H&P she continues to report palpitations and nausea, but remains awake, oriented, and hemodynamically stable.

Past Medical History

Anxiety

Celiac disease – on gluten-free diet, reportedly compliant

Migraines

No history of:

Congenital heart disease

Known arrhythmias

Diabetes, renal, or hepatic disease

Past Surgical History

None reported.

Medications

Home Medications:

Amitriptyline (dose not specified in case; taken nightly for migraines)

Hydroxyzine (dose not specified; PRN or scheduled for anxiety)

Inpatient Medications (Prior to current event):

IV fluids (e.g., D5 ½NS or similar at maintenance rate)

Ondansetron IV/PO PRN – several doses given

Prochlorperazine IV PRN – at least 1–2 doses given

Lorazepam IV PRN – may have received low dose for anxiety/nausea

Continued amitriptyline and hydroxyzine

Allergies

Medication allergies: None known.

Food allergies: Gluten intolerance (celiac disease); avoids gluten.

Family History

No known family history of congenital heart disease, arrhythmias, or sudden cardiac death at a young age.

Migraine history in a parent is possible.

Anxiety disorders present in family members.

Social History

Lives with parents, attends school.

Denies tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drug use.

No vaping.

Plays some sports and participates in school regularly when well.

Review of Systems

Constitutional: Fatigue, decreased oral intake, weight change not clearly quantified. No recent fevers or night sweats.
HEENT: No sore throat or recent URI symptoms reported. No visual changes.
Cardiovascular: Palpitations described as “heart feels weird/skipping beats.” Lightheadedness and dizziness, especially when upright. No crushing chest pain or frank syncope.
Respiratory: Denies shortness of breath, cough, or wheezing.
GI: Multiple episodes of non-bloody emesis; nausea; no diarrhea; mild diffuse abdominal discomfort. No melena or hematemesis.
GU: Decreased urine output but still voiding; no dysuria or hematuria.
Neuro: Dizziness, headaches consistent with migraine history (not currently severe). No focal neurologic deficits, no seizures.
Psych: Anxiety present, worsened by current symptoms and hospitalization. Denies active suicidal ideation.

Vital Signs

Earlier (pre-event):

BP: 104/62

HR: 88

RR: 16

SpO₂: 99% RA

Temp: 98.4°F

Current (at time of palpitations):

BP: 96/58

HR: 112 (irregular)

RR: 20

SpO₂: 96% RA

Temp: 98.6°F

Physical Examination

General:
Pale, anxious 14-year-old female, sitting up in bed, clutching an emesis bag. Appears uncomfortable but not in acute respiratory distress. Alert and cooperative.

HEENT:
Normocephalic, atraumatic. Pupils equal and reactive. Mucous membranes dry. No scleral icterus. No oral lesions.

Neck:
Supple, no JVD, no lymphadenopathy.

Cardiovascular:
Tachycardic, HR ~110–115. Rhythm irregular with occasional extra beats appreciated. No murmurs, rubs, or gallops appreciated. Peripheral pulses present, slightly thready. Capillary refill ~2–3 seconds.

Respiratory:
Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally. No wheezes, rales, or rhonchi. Normal work of breathing.

Abdomen:
Soft, mildly diffusely tender to palpation, no rebound or guarding. Non-distended. Bowel sounds present.

Extremities:
No edema or cyanosis. Warm but pale.

Neuro:
Alert and oriented ×3. Cranial nerves II–XII grossly intact. Moves all extremities spontaneously, normal strength on brief exam. No focal deficit.

Skin:
Cool, pale, no rash, no petechiae or bruising.

Psych:
Anxious affect; worried about her symptoms but engaged in conversation and able to answer questions.

Labs / Studies

Initial BMP (on admission):

Na 138

K 3.8

Cl 101

CO₂ 24

BUN/Cr within normal limits

Repeat labs (after palpitations):

Na 137

K 2.7 (low)

Cl 100

CO₂ 25

BUN/Cr within normal range

Magnesium:

Mg 1.3 (low)

EKG:

Sinus rhythm with ventricular ectopy (PVCs)

QTc 540 ms (prolonged)

No imaging yet; CXR not indicated at this time.

Assessment

14-year-old female with anxiety, celiac disease, and migraines, admitted for intractable vomiting and dehydration, now with palpitations, dizziness, irregular tachycardia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and prolonged QTc on EKG.

Key issues:

Acquired long QT syndrome with ventricular ectopy

Likely due to multiple QT-prolonging medications (amitriptyline, hydroxyzine, ondansetron, prochlorperazine) combined with electrolyte losses from vomiting → hypokalemia (K 2.7) and hypomagnesemia (Mg 1.3).

EKG shows QTc 540 ms, placing her at increased risk of dangerous arrhythmias (e.g., torsades de pointes).

Ongoing vomiting and dehydration

Poor oral intake, multiple episodes of emesis, and dry mucous membranes.

Decreased urine output but still making some urine.

Underlying anxiety, celiac disease, migraines

Anxiety contributing to distress; current medications (amitriptyline, hydroxyzine) worsen QT risk.

She is currently hemodynamically stable but at high risk for significant arrhythmia without prompt correction of underlying causes.

Problem List

Acquired long QT syndrome (QTc 540 ms) with ventricular ectopy

Hypokalemia (K 2.7) and hypomagnesemia (Mg 1.3)

Intractable vomiting and dehydration

Use of multiple QT-prolonging medications (amitriptyline, hydroxyzine, ondansetron, prochlorperazine)

Anxiety, celiac disease, migraines (chronic issues)

Plan

Acquired Long QT / Ventricular Ectopy

Discontinue all QT-prolonging medications:

Hold/stop ondansetron and prochlorperazine.

Hold amitriptyline.

Strongly consider holding hydroxyzine; avoid other QT-prolonging agents.

Place patient on continuous cardiac monitoring / telemetry.

Ensure IV access is secure.

Avoid medications that further prolong QT or lower K/Mg.

Cardiology consult for guidance on duration of monitoring, follow-up EKGs, and restarting/choosing safer alternatives for anxiety/migraine.

Electrolyte Abnormalities (K 2.7, Mg 1.3)

Replete potassium IV with appropriate pediatric dosing and telemetry (e.g., KCl IV with rate per protocol, targeting K > 4.0).

Replete magnesium IV (e.g., magnesium sulfate IV per weight-based dosing, targeting Mg ≥ 2.0).

Repeat BMP and Mg after repletion and periodically until normalized.

Maintain electrolytes in high-normal range while QT remains prolonged.

Vomiting and Dehydration

Continue IV fluids with appropriate electrolyte composition; adjust rate based on hydration status, labs, and urine output.

Avoid additional QT-prolonging antiemetics; consider non-QT-prolonging options or non-pharmacologic measures (cool cloth, slow positional changes) as tolerated.

Monitor strict intake and output, daily weights if prolonged course.

Evaluate for other causes of persistent vomiting (migraine-related, functional, or other GI pathology) if symptoms persist after initial stabilization.

Symptom Control & Safety

Treat nausea cautiously, prioritizing electrolyte correction and fluid support.

For anxiety, consider non-QT-prolonging alternatives and supportive therapy; avoid benzodiazepines unless clearly indicated and used cautiously.

Provide reassurance and clear explanations to reduce anxiety about palpitations and monitoring.

Chronic Conditions

Celiac disease: Ensure continued gluten-free diet when tolerating PO.

Migraines: Hold amitriptyline for now; consider neurology input for non-QT-prolonging prophylaxis once stabilized.

Disposition

Requires telemetry/step-down or PICU-level monitoring initially given QTc 540 ms with ectopy and electrolyte abnormalities.

Disposition to general floor only after QT has normalized/improved, electrolytes are corrected, and offending meds addressed.

Prior to discharge:

Repeat EKG to confirm QT normalization or significant improvement.

Arrange cardiology follow-up as needed.

Review medication list for future QT risk and educate family.

clinicalNotes.title: Postoperative Floor Transfer H&P
clinicalNotes.content:
S — Subjective

Demographics: Mark Casey, 60-year-old male
Chief complaint: “Severe abdominal pain” (postoperative)

History of Present Illness

60M with known CAD, HTN, and CHF presented to the ED after several days of dull upper abdominal pain that acutely worsened to severe abdominal pain with blood in the stool. Evaluation and imaging were consistent with a perforated peptic ulcer, and he received 30 mL/kg IV fluids in the ED followed by emergent operative repair. Intraoperatively he received 2 units PRBCs. He was monitored in the ICU postoperatively x ~36 hours with an uneventful course and is now admitted to the medical/surgical floor for continued postoperative management. On arrival to the floor, he reports significant incisional/abdominal pain 8/10, and he has been reluctant to ambulate due to discomfort. Denies current nausea/vomiting (NGT in place). No chest pain or dyspnea reported.

Review of Systems (positives/negatives only)

Positive: abdominal pain; limited mobility due to pain.
Negative: chest pain, shortness of breath, vomiting, fevers/chills (per patient report; afebrile on arrival).

Past History

PMH: CAD, hypertension, CHF.

PSH: Recent emergent surgery for perforated peptic ulcer (details per op note).

Medications (home): Not available on admission—med reconciliation pending.

Allergies: Not documented—verify.

Family History: Not documented.

Social History: Not documented (tobacco/alcohol/living situation/functional baseline)—obtain when pain controlled.

O — Objective

Vital signs: T 37.0°C, HR 101, BP 145/92, RR 22, SpO₂ 96% (RA)

General: Awake, uncomfortable due to pain; no acute respiratory distress.

Physical Exam

CV: Tachycardic; no additional findings provided.

Respiratory: Non-labored breathing; oxygenating well on RA.

Abdomen: Midline surgical incision clean/dry/intact with dressing. Soft, tender near incision. Hypoactive bowel sounds. JP drain with serosanguinous output.

Extremities: No findings provided; SCDs ordered.

Neuro: Alert, appropriate; no focal deficits reported.

Labs (on admission to floor)

Na 135, Cl 98, K 3.0, CO₂ 22, BUN 24, Cr 0.99, Glu 90, Ca 9.2

WBC 9, RBC 5, Hgb 13, Hct 39, Plt 250

Imaging: Pre-op imaging consistent with perforated peptic ulcer (details not provided). No new imaging available.

A — Assessment

60M with CAD/HTN/CHF, now POD#1–2 (timing approximate) s/p emergent repair of perforated peptic ulcer after ICU monitoring, transferring to floor. Primary issues: post-op abdominal pain limiting ambulation, hypokalemia, and close monitoring for postoperative complications (ileus, leak, abscess/sepsis, bleeding) given recent perforation and transfusion.

P — Plan (problem-based)
1) Perforated peptic ulcer — s/p emergent operative repair, postoperative floor management

Rationale/DDx for ongoing pain: expected postoperative/incisional pain vs ileus, anastomotic/leak, intra-abdominal abscess, ongoing bleeding. Currently afebrile, WBC normal, abdomen soft; continue close monitoring.
Diagnostics/Monitoring

Strict I&O, monitor JP output (amount/character) and NGT output.

Daily CBC, CMP; repeat BMP after potassium replacement.

Trend vitals; monitor for fever, rising WBC, worsening pain/rigidity, increasing drain output, tachycardia/hypotension.

Consider repeat CT A/P with contrast if clinical deterioration or concern for leak/abscess.
Therapeutics

NPO, NGT to low intermittent suction.

NS 100 mL/hr (reassess daily; adjust for CHF/volume status).

Zosyn 3.375 g IV q8h (continue per surgery protocol; de-escalate based on course/cultures if obtained).

Protonix 40 mg IV daily.
Disposition

Continue inpatient med/surg with surgical primary; goal: pain controlled, ambulating, bowel function returns, NGT/drains managed, tolerating diet advancement.

2) Postoperative pain — severe, limiting mobility

Rationale: Pain 8/10 with reluctance to ambulate → increased risk of atelectasis, ileus, VTE, delayed recovery.
Therapeutics

Continue morphine 2 mg IV q2h PRN pain >7; reassess efficacy/sedation/respiratory status.

Add/encourage multimodal analgesia if allowed by surgery (e.g., scheduled acetaminophen when enteral route permitted; avoid NSAIDs if ulcer risk/renal perfusion concerns).

Encourage splinting, repositioning, and early mobility with assistance once pain better controlled.
Monitoring

Sedation score, RR/O₂ sat, bowel function/ileus, nausea.

3) Hypokalemia (K 3.0)

Rationale/DDx: likely GI losses (NG suction), perioperative shifts; increases arrhythmia risk given CAD/CHF.
Diagnostics

Repeat BMP and check Mg (replete Mg if low).

Telemetry if ongoing electrolyte abnormalities/tachycardia or cardiac history warrants (consider).
Therapeutics

KCl repletion per protocol (IV given NPO/NGT); target K ≥4.0 given cardiac history.

4) CAD / HTN / CHF — perioperative medical comorbidities

Rationale: Higher risk for ischemia, arrhythmias, and fluid overload post-op. HR 101, BP 145/92. Receiving maintenance IV fluids.
Diagnostics/Monitoring

Daily weights, lung exam, I&O; monitor for edema, crackles, increasing O₂ needs.

Review home cardiac meds; med reconciliation ASAP (beta-blocker, ACEi/ARB, diuretics, statin, antiplatelet—restart when safe per surgery/bleeding risk).

Consider ECG/troponin only if symptoms or hemodynamic concern.
Therapeutics

Avoid excess fluids; adjust maintenance IVF based on volume status and urine output.

BP management: treat if persistently severe or symptomatic; otherwise optimize once home regimen clarified.

5) Postoperative blood-count monitoring — s/p 2 units PRBC intraoperatively

Rationale: Hemoglobin 13 and hematocrit 39 are concordant. JP output serosanguinous but not described as excessive.
Diagnostics

CBC daily; monitor for melena/hematochezia recurrence, tachycardia/hypotension.
Therapeutics

Transfuse only if clinically indicated (e.g., Hgb threshold per comorbidities/active bleeding).

6) VTE prophylaxis / mobility / pulmonary hygiene

Rationale: Post-op abdominal surgery + limited ambulation = high VTE/atelectasis risk.
Therapeutics

SCDs bilateral (already ordered).

Encourage early ambulation with assist; fall precautions.

Incentive spirometry, coughing/deep breathing.

7) Nausea prevention

Zofran 4 mg IV q6h PRN nausea.

PROGRESS NOTE
Author: undefined
==================================================

Postpartum Day: #0
Delivery: Spontaneous vaginal delivery

clinicalNotes.title: Admission H&P
clinicalNotes.content:
ADMISSION HISTORY AND PHYSICAL

HPI: Craig Davis is a 57-year-old man with schizophrenia, COPD requiring home oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula, and self-reported OSA. He is admitted involuntarily for worsening paranoia, disorganization and inability to care for himself. Neighbors found him confused outside without pants; he expressed a belief that his oxygen was being poisoned. He ambulates slowly and intermittently wheezes at baseline. Medication and oxygen adherence have been inconsistent. He denies current suicidal or homicidal ideation, fever, chest pain or change in sputum. History is limited by disorganization.

History: Schizophrenia, COPD and reported OSA. Surgical and family history are not established. He lives alone with limited supports. No known drug allergies are reported; verify on reconciliation.

Admission medications: Risperidone 3 mg PO at bedtime; risperidone 1 mg PO every 6 hours as needed for agitation; lorazepam 1 mg PO every 6 hours as needed for agitation; tiotropium inhaler daily, with formulation and dose to be verified. Oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula continuously.

Baseline findings: BP 132/84, HR 92, RR 18, temperature 98.2 F, SpO2 95% on 2 L/min nasal cannula. Alert, disorganized and paranoid but redirectable. Mild expiratory wheeze without crackles or increased work of breathing on prescribed oxygen. Regular heart rhythm. Abdomen soft and nontender. No peripheral edema or focal neurologic deficit.

Admission studies: CBC and CMP within normal limits: WBC 7.8, hemoglobin 14.1, platelets 260, sodium 138, potassium 4.1, creatinine 0.9, BUN 16, glucose 103 and bicarbonate 28. Chest radiograph shows chronic COPD changes without acute infiltrate, effusion or pneumothorax.

Assessment and Plan:
1. Schizophrenia with psychotic decompensation and impaired self-care. Continue risperidone 3 mg PO at bedtime and existing as-needed agitation regimen. Use verbal de-escalation and supportive redirection first. Assess sedation, extrapyramidal symptoms and medical causes of behavioral change. Monitor respiratory status carefully when sedating medications are used.
2. COPD with chronic oxygen requirement. Continue oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula and daily tiotropium. Respiratory therapy to verify inhaler strength, device and technique. Keep upright with a wedge pillow. Check vital signs and pulse oximetry at least every 4 hours and as needed. Obtain prompt medical evaluation for sustained SpO2 below 90%, increasing work of breathing or altered mental status despite prescribed oxygen.
3. Reported OSA. Clarify prior sleep evaluation and PAP prescription; avoid unnecessary sedation and monitor for sleep-related respiratory compromise.
4. Standard psychiatric safety observations, daily clinical reassessment, medication reconciliation and social-work support for safe aftercare.

clinicalNotes.title: Admission H&P
clinicalNotes.content:
ADMISSION HISTORY AND PHYSICAL

HPI: Michael Chen is a 46-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder admitted to inpatient psychiatry after being found yelling and threatening passersby. He was brought to the ED involuntarily for danger to others and inability to care for himself. In the ED he received chlorpromazine 50 mg IM and lorazepam 2 mg IM for severe agitation. After calming, he remained disorganized and required inpatient stabilization. History and review of systems are limited by psychosis. No fever, recent trauma, focal neurologic symptoms or acute medical complaint was reported on admission.

History: Schizoaffective disorder with recurrent admissions and inconsistent outpatient adherence. Other chronic medical conditions and medications require reconciliation. Cannabis use is supported by the admission urine screen. Allergies: no known drug allergies reported; verify. Housing and supports are unclear.

Admission findings: BP 128/78, HR 88, RR 17, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 98.4 F. Disheveled, alert and disorganized, with poor attention, insight and judgment. Interview reliability is limited. No focal neurologic deficit, respiratory distress, fever or rigidity is described. CBC and CMP are within normal limits. Urine drug screen is positive for cannabis.

Assessment and Plan:
1. Schizoaffective disorder with acute psychotic decompensation. Restart risperidone 3 mg PO nightly. Risperidone 1 mg PO every 4 hours as needed for agitation; lorazepam 1 mg PO every 4 hours as needed for agitation. Notify prescriber after 3 PRN doses in 24 hours. Use de-escalation first, review cumulative medication exposure, and reassess response and sedation after each dose. Prior ED IM medications were one-time treatment, not standing orders.
2. Safety and medical monitoring. Standard inpatient psychiatric precautions and daily risk reassessment. Monitor vital signs, consciousness and respiratory status with sedating medications. Evaluate new altered mental status, fever, rigidity, hypoxia or autonomic instability medically before further sedation. No routine CK or repeat metabolic testing without a new indication.
3. Medication reconciliation. Verify other chronic medications and allergies rather than restarting unspecified agents. Review QTc when escalating QT-prolonging treatment.
4. Supportive care and disposition. Structured therapeutic environment, assistance with hygiene and ADLs, psychiatric treatment and social-work assessment of housing, supports and follow-up. Offer substance-use counseling when able to engage.

The pain has been progressively persistent and is associated with decreased appetite and subjective low-grade fevers at home. She denies nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or constipation and reports normal bowel movements. She has not noted urinary symptoms. She reports regular menstrual cycles with her last menstrual period one week ago. She is not sexually active and denies concern for pregnancy or sexually transmitted infection. No prior similar episodes.

Review of Systems (positives/negatives only):
Positive for right lower quadrant abdominal pain, decreased appetite, and subjective fever. Negative for nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, dysuria, hematuria, vaginal discharge, abnormal vaginal bleeding, chest pain, dyspnea, or neurologic symptoms.

Past Surgical History: None

Social History: Denies tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drug use. Lives independently and is fully functional. Not sexually active.

BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 95 bpm, RR 18/min, afebrile, SpO₂ 100% on room air

General:
Alert, uncomfortable but not toxic-appearing

Physical Examination:

Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm

Pulmonary: Clear to auscultation bilaterally

Abdomen: Soft, nondistended with mild tenderness to palpation in the right lower quadrant; no rebound or guarding; normal bowel sounds

Neurologic: Alert and oriented, no focal deficits

Labs & Imaging:
Initial labs notable for leukocytosis with WBC 16 K/µL and left shift. Beta-hCG negative. Remaining labs unremarkable. CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast is pending at time of sign-out.

Medical Decision Making

This is a 35-year-old female with no significant past medical history presenting with two days of right lower quadrant abdominal pain, anorexia, subjective fevers, and leukocytosis with left shift, raising concern for acute appendicitis. Physical exam demonstrates localized right lower quadrant tenderness without peritoneal signs, and the patient remains hemodynamically stable and nontoxic in appearance. Pregnancy has been ruled out with a negative beta-hCG. Gynecologic pathology is considered less likely given recent menses, lack of sexual activity, and absence of pelvic or vaginal symptoms. Gastroenteritis is less likely given absence of vomiting or diarrhea. Urologic etiologies are also less likely in the absence of urinary symptoms or hematuria.

The patient has been appropriately managed with NPO status, intravenous fluids with lactated Ringer’s at 125 cc/hr, and IV fentanyl for analgesia with adequate pain control. CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast is pending to evaluate for appendicitis or alternative intra-abdominal pathology. Serial abdominal examinations will be continued while awaiting imaging. If imaging confirms appendicitis, general surgery consultation and admission for operative management will be pursued. Pending imaging results, the patient remains clinically stable at time of sign-out.

clinicalNotes.title: ED Admission H&P
clinicalNotes.content:
S — Subjective

Demographics/CC: Mr. Shao is a 65-year-old male presenting with shortness of breath and bilateral leg swelling.

HPI: He has known ischemic cardiomyopathy with HFrEF (LVEF ~25%), CAD s/p RCA stent (2018), HTN, HLD, and T2DM. Over the last 4–5 days he has had progressively worsening dyspnea and increasing bilateral lower extremity edema. He denies chest pain. He reports nonadherence with his GDMT including furosemide and increased dietary sodium intake after the holidays. On arrival he was hypoxic to 86% on room air (baseline no home oxygen) and improved to low 90s after initiation of 2L nasal cannula.

ROS (positives/negatives): Positive for dyspnea and leg swelling. Negative for chest pain. Other systems not fully elicited/documented.

PMH/PSH: Ischemic cardiomyopathy/HFrEF (EF ~25%), CAD s/p PCI to RCA (2018), HTN, HLD, T2DM. Prior PCI as above.

Medications/Allergies: Home medication list not yet fully reconciled; patient reports noncompliance including furosemide. Allergies not yet obtained.

FHx/SocHx: Not yet obtained.

O — Objective

Vital signs: Afebrile, BP 154/86, HR 88, RR 26, SpO2 92% on 2L NC.

Physical exam: He appears mildly tachypneic. Lung exam with bibasilar crackles. Extremities with 2+ bilateral pitting edema. Remaining exam not fully documented.

Diagnostics/Treatments in ED: EKG without acute ischemic changes. CXR with pulmonary edema/congestion. Labs notable for BNP 1640, K 2.8 mEq/L, sCr 1.2 mg/dL. Furosemide 60 mg IV has been ordered but has not yet been administered. Losartan 25 mg PO and correction insulin with meals are ordered. He is on 2 L nasal cannula.

MDM 

This presentation is most consistent with acute decompensated HFrEF with pulmonary edema causing acute hypoxic respiratory failure, likely precipitated by medication nonadherence (including diuretic) and increased sodium intake. Alternative diagnoses considered include ACS/ischemia, arrhythmia, pneumonia, and PE; ACS is less likely given no chest pain and a non-ischemic EKG, and infection is less likely given afebrile status and no reported infectious symptoms, though these will be reconsidered if he fails to improve with diuresis or develops new findings.

He has a new oxygen requirement and clear volume overload on exam and imaging, supporting admission-level care for continued IV diuresis, oxygen wean, and monitoring. Significant hypokalemia (K 2.8) increases dysrhythmia risk in the setting of cardiomyopathy and ongoing diuresis; plan is prompt potassium repletion with magnesium check/repletion, telemetry, and repeat BMPs to ensure correction and monitor renal function. Medicine has been paged for admission evaluation and we are awaiting call back. Cardiology has been consulted and we are waiting to hear back from Cardiology regarding management recommendations and final disposition.

Demographics: 67-year-old patient with history of insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (IDDM).
Chief Complaint: Right hip pain after fall.

History of Present Illness

67-year-old with PMH of IDDM presents after a mechanical ground-level fall with immediate right hip pain and inability to bear weight. Denies preceding chest pain, palpitations, dyspnea, dizziness, or loss of consciousness per ED history. Imaging in ED demonstrated a right hip fracture. Orthopedics consulted and plans operative repair tomorrow; patient to remain NPO after midnight. Pain currently managed with multimodal regimen. Reported mild swelling at right hip; leg noted to be mildly externally rotated with intact distal pulses. Bedtime accucheck 150.

Review of Systems (positives/negatives)

Positive for right hip pain, decreased mobility. Negative for head strike, headache, focal weakness/numbness, chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, dysuria, fevers/chills.

Past Medical History: IDDM.
Past Surgical History: Not documented.

Allergies: Not documented (verify).
Family History: Not documented.
Social History: Tobacco/alcohol/illicit use not documented. Living situation and baseline functional status not documented (verify). Sexual history not relevant to chief complaint.

O — Objective

Vital Signs (ED): Reportedly hemodynamically stable, afebrile, oxygenating well on room air (exact values not provided).
POC glucose: 150 at HS.

Physical Exam

General: Alert, in pain with movement, no acute respiratory distress.

HEENT: No reported head trauma; mucous membranes moist.

CV: Regular rhythm; no acute findings reported.

Pulm: Breathing comfortably on RA; no acute findings reported.

Abd: Soft, non-tender per ED.

MSK: R hip: mild swelling/tenderness, mild external rotation; limited ROM due to pain.

Neuro: Awake/interactive; no focal deficits reported.

Vascular/Skin: DP pulses intact on right; no skin breakdown noted.

Labs / Imaging

CBC: WNL.

CMP: Glucose 207, creatinine 1.3, otherwise WNL.

INR: WNL.

Imaging: Right hip fracture on ED imaging (fracture subtype not specified).

A — Assessment & P — Plan

Primary clinical impression: Acute right hip fracture after mechanical GLF in a patient with IDDM, planned for operative repair tomorrow; needs perioperative medical optimization, glycemic management, analgesia, and VTE prophylaxis.

1) Right hip fracture (acute), mechanical GLF

Rationale/DDx: Imaging-confirmed fracture after low-energy mechanical fall; consider fragility fracture/osteoporosis risk given age.
Plan:

Admit to Medicine for perioperative management; Ortho primary surgical plan for OR tomorrow.

NPO after midnight; ensure Type & Screen (and crossmatch per Ortho).

Pre-op: EKG now; CXR only if clinically indicated (symptoms/abnormal exam).

Maintain non–weight bearing RLE; fall precautions.

PT/OT post-op; early mobilization when cleared by Ortho.

Evaluate bone health: 25-OH Vit D, calcium/phos; start calcium/vitamin D if no contraindication; outpatient osteoporosis workup/therapy post-discharge.

2) Acute pain due to fracture

Rationale: Significant nociceptive pain; avoid oversedation in older adult.
Plan:

Multimodal analgesia: scheduled acetaminophen (max 3g/day if no liver disease).

Opioid PRN (e.g., low-dose oxycodone or IV hydromorphone for breakthrough).

Avoid/limit NSAIDs given creatinine 1.3 and peri-op bleeding risk (unless Ortho OK).

Bowel regimen (senna +/- PEG) while on opioids.

3) Diabetes mellitus (IDDM) — perioperative glycemic control

Rationale: Hyperglycemia (207 on CMP); will be NPO; risk of hypoglycemia if full prandial insulin given while NPO.
Plan:

Accuchecks AC/HS today; when NPO, q6h.

Basal insulin: continue glargine but reduce dose night before surgery (commonly 50–80% of home dose) to prevent hypoglycemia while NPO; adjust based on trends.

Prandial insulin: give lispro with meals only; hold when NPO.

Correctional insulin (SSI): add per protocol.

Target peri-op glucose typically 140–180; avoid hypoglycemia.

4) Creatinine 1.3 — mild renal impairment (AKI vs baseline CKD)

Rationale: Mild elevation; baseline unknown; peri-op risk with dehydration/nephrotoxins.
Plan:

Trend BMP daily; review prior records for baseline creatinine.

Maintain euvolemia; consider maintenance IV fluids overnight while NPO if intake inadequate.

Avoid nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, IV contrast unless necessary); renally dose meds as needed.

5) Perioperative risk / medical optimization

Rationale: Needs surgical clearance/optimization; limited history available.
Plan:

Clarify baseline functional capacity/METs, cardiac history, OSA, prior anesthesia issues.

If no active cardiac conditions and EKG unremarkable, proceed per guideline-based assessment.

Ensure Hgb stable pre-op; repeat CBC in AM if needed per Ortho/anesthesia.

6) VTE prophylaxis

Rationale: High VTE risk with hip fracture and immobility.
Plan:

SCDs now.

Pharmacologic prophylaxis (e.g., LMWH) per Ortho protocol; coordinate hold timing pre-op and resume post-op when safe.

clinicalNotes.title: ED Evaluation — Tera Bransley
clinicalNotes.content:
S — Subjective
Chief Complaint

Agitation, altered mental status

History of Present Illness

Tera Bransley is a 34-year-old female with a history of schizoaffective disorder, opioid use disorder on methadone, and recreational methamphetamine use who was brought to the ED via EMS after being found outside a gas station screaming and acting erratically. Per EMS, the patient was agitated and combative on scene. On arrival to the ED, she remained severely agitated with hyperactivity, pressured and tangential speech, and was unable to provide a coherent history. Due to concern for patient and staff safety, she required chemical sedation with droperidol and lorazepam to facilitate evaluation. Initial diagnostic workup revealed stimulant intoxication with associated rhabdomyolysis, electrolyte derangements, and mild acute kidney injury. Medicine was consulted for possible admission.

Review of Systems (limited by mental status)

Positive: Agitation, confusion, restlessness

Negative: No reported chest pain, shortness of breath, focal neurologic deficits, or seizure activity per EMS

Past Medical History

Schizoaffective disorder

Opioid use disorder on methadone

Methamphetamine use

Medications

Methadone 30 mg PO daily maintenance; verify last administration before dosing.

Allergies

No known drug allergies documented

Social History

Polysubstance use including methamphetamine

Other details unable to obtain

O — Objective
Vital Signs

BP: 140/74 mmHg

HR: 115 bpm

RR: 22 bpm

Temp: 99.6°F (37.6°C)

SpO₂: 98% on room air

General

Agitated, hyperactive female requiring chemical sedation for evaluation.

Physical Exam

HEENT: Pupils dilated, equal, reactive

CV: Tachycardic, regular rhythm

Pulmonary: Clear bilaterally, no distress

Abdomen: Soft, non-tender

Neuro: Awake but confused; oriented to self only; pressured, tangential speech; moving all extremities; no focal deficits

Skin: Warm, no trauma noted

Diagnostics

Labs:

CK 5,600 U/L

Creatinine 1.3 mg/dL

Potassium 2.8 mEq/L

Magnesium 0.8 mEq/L

UDS positive for methamphetamine and methadone

Imaging:

CT head: No acute intracranial abnormality

MDM — Medical Decision Making

This 34-year-old female presents with severe agitation and altered mental status. Initial differential diagnosis included acute stimulant intoxication, primary psychiatric decompensation, intracranial pathology, infection, and metabolic derangements. Given her known substance use history, marked psychomotor agitation, dilated pupils, tachycardia, and positive urine toxicology, acute methamphetamine intoxication was felt to be the primary driver of her presentation, with possible contribution from underlying schizoaffective disorder.

Due to the severity of agitation and inability to safely evaluate the patient, chemical sedation with droperidol and lorazepam was required. CT head was obtained to evaluate for intracranial pathology and was negative. Laboratory evaluation revealed significant rhabdomyolysis (CK 5,600 U/L), mild acute kidney injury, and severe hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia, likely secondary to prolonged agitation, hyperactivity, and dehydration in the setting of stimulant use.

The patient was started on maintenance IV fluids (LR at 100 cc/hr) for renal protection and treatment of rhabdomyolysis, with plans for electrolyte repletion and close monitoring. Given the degree of metabolic derangement, AKI, and need for continued IV fluids, telemetry, and serial labs, the patient is not appropriate for discharge from the ED.

Medicine consultation is pending to determine inpatient admission for continued management of toxic-metabolic encephalopathy, rhabdomyolysis, electrolyte abnormalities, and monitoring for complications. The patient remains hemodynamically stable but requires close observation given polysubstance use and altered mental status.

clinicalNotes.title: Admission H&P — COVID-19 with Hypoxemia
clinicalNotes.content:
ADMISSION HISTORY AND PHYSICAL
Linda Poppy — Room 203
Older adult woman with obesity and former tobacco use; no known drug allergies.

Chief complaint: Shortness of breath.
HPI: Several days of cough, subjective fever and dyspnea after a sick contact. SARS-CoV-2 testing is positive. In the ED oxygen saturation was 91% on room air at rest and briefly fell to 87% with ambulation. Chest radiograph showed no focal consolidation. An initial Paxlovid dose was given in the ED; she is admitted because of hypoxemia and is transitioned to an inpatient regimen. No chronic home medications are reported.
Exam on admission: BP 128/75, HR 110, RR 14, temperature 100.2 F. Alert, dyspneic with exertion. Diminished breath sounds at the bases with scattered expiratory wheezes; no edema or focal neurologic deficit. Oxygen saturation improves to 94% on 2 L/min nasal cannula.
Labs: WBC 13 K/uL; remaining CBC, CMP and lactate are within normal limits. SARS-CoV-2 positive. CXR without focal consolidation.

Assessment and plan:
1. COVID-19 with hypoxemia requiring low-flow oxygen. Oxygen by nasal cannula titrated to SpO2 92–96%, continuous pulse oximetry and vital signs every 4 hours. Remdesivir 200 mg IV on day 1, then 100 mg IV daily on days 2–5 or until discharge, with hepatic testing and clinical monitoring. Dexamethasone 6 mg PO daily for up to 10 days or until discharge. Stop Paxlovid after transition; no concurrent antiviral course.
2. Supportive care: regular diet as tolerated; acetaminophen 650 mg PO every 6 hours PRN fever or pain, maximum 3 g/day. Enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily for inpatient VTE prophylaxis with normal renal function and no bleeding contraindication.
3. Reassess promptly for increasing oxygen requirement, respiratory distress or instability. Escalation of respiratory support and level of care will depend on subsequent clinical assessment.
Code status: Full code.

Demographics:
Mrs. Irene Fisher, 82-year-old female

Chief Complaint:
Headache and neck pain after motor vehicle collision

History of Present Illness:
Mrs. Fisher is an 82-year-old female with a past medical history significant for atrial fibrillation on apixaban and hypertension who presented to the emergency department after a motor vehicle collision. She was the restrained front-seat passenger in a vehicle struck by an oncoming car traveling approximately 45 mph with airbag deployment. She denies loss of consciousness. She reports immediate onset of diffuse pain, most notable in the head and neck. She denies focal weakness, numbness, vision changes, chest pain, shortness of breath, or abdominal pain. EMS placed a cervical collar prior to arrival. She has remained awake, alert, and answering questions appropriately since the event.

Review of Systems (positives and negatives only):
Positive for headache and neck pain. Negative for loss of consciousness, dizziness, vision changes, focal weakness, numbness, chest pain, dyspnea, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or extremity pain.

Past Medical History:

Atrial fibrillation

Hypertension

Past Surgical History:

Not documented

Medications:

Apixaban

Antihypertensive medications (unspecified)

Allergies:

No known drug allergies

Social History:

Tobacco: denies

Alcohol: denies; ethanol negative

Functional status: ambulatory at baseline

O — Objective

Vital Signs:

Stable; heart rate within normal limits, irregularly irregular

General Appearance:

Awake, alert, cervical collar in place, uncomfortable but no acute distress

Physical Examination:

HEENT: Normocephalic, atraumatic

Neck: Cervical collar in place; paraspinal cervical tenderness; no midline spinous tenderness or step-offs

Cardiovascular: Irregularly irregular rhythm, normal rate

Pulmonary: Clear to auscultation bilaterally

Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, non-distended

Musculoskeletal: No deformities; full strength in all extremities

Neurologic: Alert and oriented; cranial nerves intact; strength 5/5 and sensation intact in all extremities

Skin: No external signs of trauma

Diagnostics:

Labs: CBC, CMP within normal limits; INR 1.3 (on apixaban); ethanol negative

Imaging (pending):

CT head without contrast

CT cervical spine without contrast

CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast

MDM — Medical Decision Making

This is an 82-year-old anticoagulated female presenting after a high-speed motor vehicle collision with head and neck pain. Given the significant mechanism of injury, advanced age, and use of apixaban, the patient is high risk for occult intracranial hemorrhage, cervical spine injury, and internal blunt trauma despite a reassuring neurologic examination and hemodynamic stability.

A trauma imaging workup was initiated, including CT head without contrast to evaluate for intracranial hemorrhage, CT cervical spine without contrast to assess for cervical spine injury, and CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast to evaluate for thoracic or intra-abdominal injury. Cervical spine precautions were maintained with a cervical collar.

Laboratory evaluation including CBC, CMP, and coagulation studies was obtained; results were within normal limits with INR 1.3, consistent with apixaban use. Ethanol level was negative. The patient was started on IV lactated Ringer’s at 75 cc/hr for maintenance hydration. Pain control was provided with non-NSAID analgesia.

Given the patient’s anticoagulation status and high-risk mechanism, she will require close monitoring with serial neurologic examinations while awaiting imaging results. Anticoagulation is being held pending trauma imaging. Admitted for elective colostomy reversal. At baseline without fever, abdominal pain, vomiting, chest pain or dyspnea; ostomy functioning normally. No known drug allergies.

clinicalNotes.title: MFM Progress — Hospital Day 2, Before Overnight Symptoms
clinicalNotes.content:
MATERNAL-FETAL MEDICINE PROGRESS NOTE — Hospital day 2
Mo'Nique Alvin — L&D 03
G1P0 at 26 weeks 3 days at admission, hospitalized for marked hyperglycemia after late entry to prenatal care. Admission glucose 368 mg/dL; no acidosis or clinical ketosis. Other admission bloodwork reassuring. Fasting glucose this morning 140 mg/dL; remaining values near target. No fever, contractions, vaginal bleeding or fluid leakage at this assessment.
T 36.8 C, BP 118/72, HR 86, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air. Comfortable, gravid nontender abdomen, no respiratory distress or focal deficit.
Assessment: Diabetes in pregnancy requiring insulin; severe presentation raises concern for previously unrecognized pregestational diabetes.
Plan: NPH 28 units SC each morning and increase bedtime NPH from 10 to 14 units. Lispro 14 units SC before breakfast and 10 units SC before dinner, given with the meal; hold nutritional lispro if the meal is not eaten. Additional lispro correction before meals only: glucose 141–180, 1 unit; 181–220, 2; 221–260, 3; 261–300, 4; above 300, 5 units and notify provider/check ketones. No additional rapid-acting correction within 4 hours of a prior lispro dose. Check glucose fasting, before meals, 1 hour after meals and at bedtime; pregnancy targets fasting below 95 and 1-hour postmeal below 140. Notify MFM for persistent elevations and titrate scheduled doses; do not automatically correct a 1-hour postmeal value.
Carbohydrate-consistent pregnancy diet; diabetes education and nutrition consultation. Fetal echocardiogram remains pending. Continue prenatal vitamin and routine fetal assessment. Discharge anticipated on day 3 if stable, after education and outpatient insulin supplies/follow-up are arranged.

ED ADMISSION HISTORY AND PHYSICAL

Assessment: Suspected non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome, including unstable angina. The initial negative troponin does not establish NSTEMI; repeat testing and clinical reassessment are required.

clinicalNotes.content:

64-year-old man with hypertension and type2diabetes presents with one week of intermittent dizziness, lightheadedness, palpitations and mild dyspnea. Episodes last minutes and resolve spontaneously. No chest pain, syncope, focal neurologic symptoms or recent illness. Asymptomatic on initial ED assessment.
Home regimen: lisinopril10mgPOdaily and metformin500mgPOtwice daily with meals. No known drug allergies.
Initial exam: Comfortable, normal vital signs, regular heart rhythm, clear lungs, no edema or focal deficit. Initial ECG normal sinus rhythm. CBC,CMP,TSH and troponin unremarkable; chest radiograph normal. Telemetry captured a brief irregular rhythm during symptoms, without a sustained tachyarrhythmia documented on the initial ECG.
Assessment: Intermittent palpitations/presyncope; arrhythmia under evaluation.
Plan: Cardiology consulted and recommends overnight telemetry observation. Continuous rhythm monitoring, symptom-rhythm correlation, routine vital signs and fall precautions. Continue lisinopril10mgdaily if BP/renal function permit and metformin500mgBID with meals while eating and clinically stable; hold metformin for acute illness, renal dysfunction or fasting/procedure. Glucose checks before meals and bedtime. Obtain ECG during recurrent symptoms and reassess stability promptly. Sustained atrial fibrillation and event-specific therapy are not present at this baseline.

clinicalNotes.content:
ADMISSION HISTORY AND PHYSICAL

HPI: Juan Martinez is a 34-year-old man with opioid use disorder and depression, admitted voluntarily after making suicidal statements to police. He reports fentanyl use of 2–3 bags daily, with last use about 24 hours before arrival. He was initially somnolent but arousable in the ED, received IV fluids and was observed until sufficiently awake for psychiatric admission. At admission he has mild opioid-withdrawal symptoms, including yawning, chills, mild gastrointestinal discomfort and anxiety; COWS is 10. He received clonidine 0.1 mg PO with partial relief. No buprenorphine induction has been ordered.

History: Depression and severe opioid use disorder. Prior outpatient antidepressant adherence has been inconsistent. No known chronic medical illness or allergies reported; verify. Housing and social supports are limited.

Admission findings: BP 128/80, HR 76, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 98.4 F. Awake and oriented, mildly uncomfortable, without respiratory distress, confusion or focal deficit. Interview supports recent suicidal statements in the context of substance use and distress; perform ongoing assessment of intent and safety. CBC and CMP are normal. Urine screen is positive for fentanyl.

Assessment and Plan:
1. Opioid use disorder with mild withdrawal at admission. Clonidine 0.1 mg PO every 6 hours as needed for withdrawal symptoms; hold for SBP below 100 mmHg, HR below 60, dizziness or symptomatic hypotension. Ondansetron 4 mg PO every 8 hours as needed for nausea. Loperamide for diarrhea: 4 mg PO initially, then 2 mg after each subsequent loose stool, maximum 16 mg/day. Encourage fluids and light food.
2. Monitor COWS and vital signs every 4 hours and as needed; reassess about 1 hour after clonidine. Notify clinician for worsening symptoms, inability to hydrate, hypotension, confusion or respiratory depression. Evaluate readiness and timing for medication treatment of opioid use disorder with the patient; induction requires a separate clinical assessment and order.
3. Depression and recent suicidal ideation. Continue sertraline 50 mg PO daily. Standard psychiatric safety observations, daily risk assessment and individualized safety planning.
4. Social work for housing and treatment access, outpatient addiction/psychiatric follow-up, recovery resources, overdose education and a discharge naloxone plan.

Admission CIWA-Ar 9 with mild tremor and anxiety. Alert and oriented; no seizure, confusion, hallucinations, head trauma or focal neurologic symptoms at admission.

Exam: BP 132/86, HR 96, RR 18, SpO2 98%, temperature 98.6 F. Anxious and mildly tremulous, cooperative. Regular heart rhythm, no respiratory distress. Alert and oriented, without focal deficit or rigidity. Linear thought process; recent suicidal statements, impaired judgment.

Assessment/Plan:
1. Early alcohol withdrawal. CIWA-Ar and vital signs every 4 hours, reassess 1 hour after benzodiazepine. Lorazepam 1 mg PO every 4 hours PRN CIWA 8-15; hold for oversedation/respiratory depression. Prompt physician reassessment and escalation for CIWA >15, hallucinations, seizure or unstable vital signs. Seizure, aspiration and fall precautions.
2. Nutritional/electrolyte support. Thiamine 100 mg IV daily for 3-5 days then PO, folic acid 1 mg PO daily, multivitamin daily. Do not delay urgent glucose for thiamine. Oral fluids and diet as tolerated; assess need for IV fluids if intake inadequate. Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 2 hours once and potassium chloride 40 mEq PO once; reassess electrolytes after replacement. Ondansetron 4 mg PO every 8 hours PRN nausea.

Admit to inpatient psychiatry

Initiate/titrate clozapine per protocol

Weekly CBC/ANC monitoring during the first six months of treatment, per current prescribing information; continue clinical monitoring.

Continue bowel regimen with docusate/senna and PEG

Monitor for clozapine adverse effects including constipation, orthostasis, myocarditis, and neutropenia

Standard safety checks and ongoing psychiatric stabilization

clinicalNotes.title: Psychiatry Progress — Day 21 Morning
clinicalNotes.content:
PSYCHIATRY PROGRESS NOTE — Hospital day 21, morning
Lucan Mireles — Room 310
Reports improvement in auditory hallucinations after three weeks of clozapine titration; current dose 250 mg nightly. Calm and participating in care. Mild constipation controlled with senna and polyethylene glycol. No fever, sore throat, chest pain or dyspnea at this assessment.
BP 122/78, HR 88, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 98.3 F. Alert, calm, blunted affect; no rigidity or abnormal movements. Cardiopulmonary examination unremarkable. Most recent weekly CBC: WBC 5.2 K/uL, ANC 2,800 cells/uL; CMP within normal limits.
Assessment: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia improving on clozapine; constipation controlled.
Plan: Continue clozapine 250 mg PO nightly and bowel regimen. Weekly CBC/ANC monitoring during the first six months; continue vital-sign, bowel-function and medication-tolerance assessment, psychiatric safety checks and discharge planning.

clinicalNotes.title: Admission H&P
clinicalNotes.content:
ADMISSION HISTORY AND PHYSICAL
Ethan Morales — Room 408

Chief complaint: Left foot redness and pain.
HPI: Adolescent boy with type 1 diabetes admitted for localized cellulitis surrounding a left foot blister. No fever, vomiting, abdominal pain or systemic symptoms at presentation. Eating and drinking normally. No admission evidence of DKA. Home basal-bolus insulin is continued.
History: Type 1 diabetes. No known drug allergies. Lives with family. Admission weight 45 kg.
Medications: Glargine 18 units SC nightly. Lispro 1 unit per 15 g carbohydrate with meals and correction 1 unit per 50 mg/dL above 150; round down to whole units. No correction more often than every 4 hours.
Exam: BP 110/68, HR 98, RR 18, temperature 98.4 F, oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Alert, comfortable and well hydrated. Lungs clear; regular heart rhythm. Abdomen soft and nontender. Localized left foot erythema and tenderness without fluctuance or drainage. Distal perfusion intact.
Admission data: WBC 12 K/uL, hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL, platelets 280 K/uL. Na 139, K 4.1, Cl 107, bicarbonate 22, anion gap 10, BUN 12, creatinine 0.6 mg/dL, glucose 92 mg/dL. Beta-hydroxybutyrate 0.1 mmol/L; HbA1c 8.1%.
Assessment: Localized left foot cellulitis in a child with type 1 diabetes; no systemic illness or DKA.
Plan: Cefazolin 1 g IV every 8 hours. Follow foot examination. MRI of the left foot planned for the next morning with sedation; NPO after midnight. Continue glargine 18 units nightly. Lispro meal coverage and correction as above; hold nutritional lispro while NPO and use correction only every 4 hours. D5NS at 75 mL/hour while NPO. Check glucose before meals and at bedtime, or every 4 hours while NPO. Acetaminophen 500 mg PO every 6 hours as needed for pain or fever. Pediatric endocrine consultation for peri-procedural diabetes management.

clinicalNotes.content:

Author: undefined

PEDIATRIC ENDOCRINOLOGY CONSULTATION — Hospital day 1, evening
Reason: Type 1 diabetes management during fasting for sedated foot MRI.
Ethan Morales is admitted with left foot cellulitis and is clinically stable. He is eating without vomiting. Weight 45 kg. No ketosis or acidosis at admission; bicarbonate 22, anion gap 10, beta-hydroxybutyrate 0.1 mmol/L. HbA1c 8.1%. Glucose has been acceptable during daytime monitoring. No symptoms of hypoglycemia at this assessment.
Home regimen reviewed: glargine 18 units SC nightly; lispro 1 unit per 15 g carbohydrate and correction 1 unit per 50 mg/dL above 150, rounded down to whole units.
Plan: Continue glargine tonight. Give meal insulin only with carbohydrate intake; hold nutritional lispro after NPO begins at midnight. Correction-only lispro every 4 hours while NPO, with no stacking within 4 hours. Begin D5NS at 75 mL/hour while NPO and monitor glucose every 4 hours. Notify the medical team for symptoms or glucose below 70; follow pediatric hypoglycemia protocol. Review insulin and dextrose needs after imaging and resumption of meals.

medicalOrders.order_name: Nursing - Oxygen, respiratory monitoring, and admission care
medicalOrders.instructions:
Order for: Oxygen, respiratory monitoring, and admission care
Requested action: Oxygen via nasal cannula continuously at 2 L/min; titrate to maintain SpO2 above 92%. Continuous pulse oximetry. Respiratory assessments and vital signs every 4 hours and as needed, including work of breathing, mental status, and oxygen requirement. Notify physician promptly for worsening hypoxemia, fatigue, decreased air movement, or increasing oxygen/nebulizer requirements. Regular diet; activity as tolerated. Maintain peripheral IV saline lock.
Notes: Admission baseline care for asthma exacerbation with pneumonia.

Location: chest, PA and lateral views. Indication: admission evaluation for fever, cough, dyspnea, and asthma exacerbation; concern for community-acquired pneumonia. Baseline study before the overnight deterioration. Show a focal right lower lobe airspace opacity consistent with pneumonia, without pleural effusion or pneumothorax.

medicalOrders.order_name: Respiratory Therapy - Acute asthma exacerbation with pneumonia
medicalOrders.instructions:
Order for: Acute asthma exacerbation with pneumonia
Requested action: Assess respiratory status and bronchodilator response. Obtain bedside peak expiratory flow before and after bronchodilator treatment if patient can perform safely; document trend. Assist with nebulizer delivery, oxygen titration to SpO2 above 92%, and inhaler/spacer education. Notify physician for fatigue, reduced air movement, or worsening oxygen need.

medicalOrders.order_name: Case Management - Controller-inhaler access and discharge planning
medicalOrders.instructions:
Order for: Controller-inhaler access and discharge planning
Requested action: Coordinate with social work for insurance assistance and medication-access programs. Patient ran out of Advair because of cost. Identify affordable ICS-containing controller therapy and rescue inhaler, confirm access before discharge, and arrange primary-care/pulmonology follow-up, spacer education, and a written asthma action plan.

medicalOrders.order_name: Nursing - Admission SBO care and monitoring
medicalOrders.instructions:
Order for: Admission SBO care and monitoring
Requested action: NPO including medications. Maintain existing nasogastric tube to low intermittent suction; document output and character. Strict intake/output and urine output, target greater than 0.5 mL/kg/hour. Vital signs and abdominal assessments every 4 hours; notify surgical team for worsening pain, guarding, persistent tachycardia, oliguria, or hemodynamic change. Continue ordered IV maintenance fluids. Hold oral antihypertensives while NPO with borderline blood pressure. This is baseline care before any subsequent tube-displacement event.

Location: abdomen and pelvis, without IV contrast because of acute kidney injury (creatinine 2.4). Indication: admission evaluation of abdominal distension, pain and vomiting with prior laparotomies; suspected adhesive small-bowel obstruction. Baseline simulation finding: dilated small-bowel loops with a transition point consistent with adhesive SBO; no free air or closed-loop configuration. Noncontrast study cannot reliably assess bowel-wall enhancement/ischemia. This is the initial admission study, not imaging after later NG-tube displacement.
Scheduled fracture pain control: 1,000 mg PO every 8 hours; maximum 3,000 mg/day from all acetaminophen sources. May take with small sip of water while otherwise NPO if permitted by surgical team.

Give 2.5 mg PO every 6 hours as needed for moderate-to-severe fracture pain; reassess effect and sedation. Hold for respiratory rate below 12/min or excessive sedation. May take with small sip of water while otherwise NPO if permitted by surgical team.
Give 8.6 mg PO nightly for prevention of opioid-associated constipation. Hold for loose stools. Resume enteral bowel regimen when permitted by NPO/surgical plan.
Give 17 g PO daily dissolved in water for opioid-associated constipation. Hold for loose stools; start when enteral intake is allowed.

Order for: T3 fracture admission precautions
Requested action: Strict bedrest and spinal precautions; no out-of-bed activity until cleared by neurosurgery. Neurologic checks and vital signs every 4 hours. Fall precautions, SCDs for VTE prophylaxis, strict intake/output, and incentive spirometry 10 breaths hourly while awake. NPO pending MRI and surgical plan; oral analgesics with small sips only if surgical team permits, otherwise request parenteral analgesia. Notify team for new weakness, numbness, bowel/bladder dysfunction, uncontrolled pain, or excessive sedation. PT/OT and orthostatic vital signs only after spine clearance. Pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis requires neurosurgical clearance.

Order for: COVID-19 admission respiratory care
Requested action: Continuous pulse oximetry. Supplemental oxygen by nasal cannula at 1–2 L/min as needed, titrate to maintain SpO2 at least 92%. Vital signs and respiratory assessments every 4 hours and as needed; notify physician for escalating oxygen requirement, persistent hypoxemia, or increased work of breathing. COVID transmission-based precautions per facility policy. Regular diet as tolerated; assist with activity because of exertional hypoxemia.
AS NEEDED only: acetaminophen 650 mg PO every 6 hours as needed for fever or mild pain. Maximum 3,000 mg/day from all sources.
Give 650 mg PO every 6 hours AS NEEDED for fever above 38.5 C (101.3 F). Maximum 3,000 mg acetaminophen from all sources in 24 hours.

Location: chest, PA and lateral. Indication: initial admission evaluation of cough, fever and dyspnea with COVID-19. Source-defined baseline chest radiograph is clear, with no focal consolidation, pleural effusion, or pneumothorax. Do not use later overnight deterioration findings.

Order for: RLE infection admission care
Requested action: Elevate affected limb, mark erythema borders, and assess wound daily and with dressing changes per surgery. Vital signs every 4 hours; monitor intake/output and notify physician for rapidly spreading erythema, pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, fever, hypotension, or new chest pain. Verify tetanus immunization status. Use mechanical VTE prophylaxis on unaffected leg if pharmacologic prophylaxis is held for procedure; coordinate medication prophylaxis with surgical plan.
Give 5 mg PO every 6 hours as needed for severe leg/wound pain. Hold for respiratory rate below 12/min or excessive sedation; reassess pain and sedation.
Establish peripheral IV access.

Vancomycin 15 mg/kg per dose IV every 12 hours using actual body weight for purulent cellulitis/abscess. Pharmacy to verify weight, renal function, dose in mg, infusion duration, and monitoring before administration; adjust per pharmacokinetic protocol. Do not interpret this as 15 mg total.
Ceftriaxone 1 g IV every 24 hours for cellulitis/abscess per admission combination regimen. Review cultures and narrow therapy when appropriate.

medicalOrders.instructions:
Order for: Vancomycin dosing and medication reconciliation
Requested action: Verify actual body weight and renal function, calculate vancomycin dose in mg and infusion duration, and adjust dose/interval with therapeutic monitoring per protocol. Reconcile home CAD medications, including antiplatelet and statin; verify allergies and coordinate perioperative antiplatelet plan with surgery.

medicalOrders.order_name: General Surgery - RLE cellulitis and abscess source control
medicalOrders.instructions:
Order for: RLE cellulitis and abscess source control
Requested action: Evaluate and manage right lower-extremity abscess requiring incision/drainage or debridement. Confirm operative status; if already debrided, direct packing and postoperative wound care. Obtain deep wound culture at source control if not already collected. Coordinate perioperative VTE and antiplatelet plan.
AS NEEDED: 650 mg PO every 6 hours for mild pain or fever. Maximum acetaminophen 3,000 mg/day from all sources.
Give 8.6 mg PO nightly while receiving opioids. Hold for loose stools.

medicalOrders.instructions:
Order for: Cholecystitis admission care and IV fluids
Requested action: NPO pending surgical plan; hold oral medicines if strictly NPO. Infuse 0.9% sodium chloride IV at 125 mL/hour continuously, reassess volume status and urine output each shift and notify physician for overload or oliguria. Strict intake/output, vital signs and abdominal assessments every 4 hours. SCDs for VTE prophylaxis. Follow surgical team for possible cholecystectomy tomorrow and reconcile perioperative medication plan. Catalog limitation: saline medication entries lack a frequency; this written infusion order specifies the intended rate.

Morphine 4 mg IV every 4 hours as needed for severe abdominal pain while NPO. Hold for respiratory rate below 12/min or excessive sedation. Do not give concurrently with oxycodone for the same pain episode; reassess response.

Give oxycodone 5 mg PO every 6 hours as needed for moderate pain only when oral medications are permitted. Hold while strictly NPO, for respiratory rate below 12/min, or excessive sedation. Do not give concurrently with IV morphine for the same pain episode.

Location: right upper quadrant abdomen. Indication: initial admission RUQ pain, Murphy sign, fever and leukocytosis. Source-defined initial ultrasound is consistent with acute calculous cholecystitis: gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening, small pericholecystic fluid and positive sonographic Murphy sign. No biliary duct dilatation. Baseline before overnight deterioration.

Preoperative admission type and screen. Fictional baseline: O positive, antibody screen negative. Exact blood group was not specified in case source; author-created simulation value. This is not a transfusion order.
Give insulin glargine 15 units subcutaneously once daily AT BEDTIME, admission reduced basal regimen per H&P. Monitor glucose and reassess daily. Do not substitute home 45-unit dose.

medicalOrders.order_name: General - Insulin lispro — mealtime and correction regimen
medicalOrders.instructions:
Order for: Insulin lispro — mealtime and correction regimen
Requested action: Insulin lispro 5 units subcutaneously THREE TIMES DAILY WITH MEALS; hold nutritional dose when NPO or meal omitted. Add sensitive correction dose before meals: BG ≤150, 0 units; 151–200, 1 unit; 201–250, 2 units; 251–300, 3 units; 301–350, 4 units; 351–400, 5 units; >400, 6 units and notify physician. At bedtime give correction only: BG ≤200, 0 units; 201–250, 1 unit; 251–300, 2 units; >300, 3 units and notify physician if >400. If NPO, stop nutritional insulin and request q4–6-hour correction plan. Hold rapid-acting insulin for BG <70 and treat per hypoglycemia protocol; recheck in 15 minutes. Avoid stacking rapid-acting doses within 4 hours. Catalog offers only qHS for lispro; use this explicit written regimen pending catalog correction.

medicalOrders.order_name: Nursing - Hyperglycemia, hyponatremia and possible CHF monitoring
medicalOrders.instructions:
Order for: Hyperglycemia, hyponatremia and possible CHF monitoring
Requested action: Fluid restriction 2,000 mL/day; no maintenance IV fluids. Consistent-carbohydrate diet. POC glucose before meals and at bedtime; notify for BG <70 or >400. Hypoglycemia: if alert and able to swallow, give 20 g rapid carbohydrate; if unable to take oral intake with IV access, give dextrose 50% 25 mL IV per protocol; recheck glucose every 15 minutes and repeat until ≥100, notify physician. Strict intake/output, daily standing weight when safe, telemetry, vital signs every 4 hours. Monitor mental status and respiratory status; notify for new confusion, seizure, dyspnea or hypoxemia. Review sodium correction and avoid rise above 6–8 mmol/L in 24 hours.

Location: 12-lead ECG. Indication: initial evaluation of hyperglycemia, hyponatremia and suspected volume overload/heart failure. Plausible baseline simulation: sinus rhythm 85 bpm, no acute ischemic ST changes. No later-event findings.

Vancomycin 15 mg/kg per dose IV every 12 hours using actual body weight. Pharmacy to verify weight and renal function, calculate total mg and infusion duration, and adjust dosing/monitoring per protocol before administration.

Location: chest PA/lateral. Indication: admission orthopnea/possible CHF, BNP 1400. Plausible initial simulation finding: mild cardiomegaly without focal pneumonia, large effusion, or frank alveolar pulmonary edema. This is baseline before overnight laboratory reassessment; do not create later case deterioration.

Give 5 mg PO every 6 hours as needed for moderate-to-severe hand pain. Hold for respiratory rate below 12/min or excessive sedation.
AS NEEDED: 650 mg PO every 6 hours for mild pain or fever. Maximum 3,000 mg/day from all sources.

Requested action: Vital signs and right-hand neurovascular checks every 4 hours; elevate hand and monitor erythema, swelling, pain, drainage, perfusion and sensation. Notify physician for progression or systemic symptoms. NPO after midnight for planned I&D; coordinate essential medications with surgical team. Screen and report withdrawal symptoms without assuming substance or withdrawal treatment.
